title: Business case: which product, which heading, which role
blurb: Place scenario information under the right business case heading or approach, and match business case actions to the right role.
question: Fernhollow Foods forecasts £6 million of branded sales a year by year three. Under which business case heading does this belong, and which role must show the business that it is on track?

teach.h: Sorting justification facts into the right drawer
teach.body: Formally, the business case practice uses four management products: the project brief, the business case, the benefits management approach and the sustainability management approach. In plain English: a launch pad for initiation, the argument for spending the money, the plan for proving the gains, and the plan for hitting the green targets. Practitioner matching sets hand you a fact from the scenario and ask which product, and which heading inside it, should hold it.

head: Product
Holds
Created
teach.caption: SU = starting up a project; IP = initiating a project. The business case is then updated at each stage boundary and in closing.

head: Heading
What it holds
Fernhollow Kitchen example
rows: £6m branded sales a year by year 3
11 months to launch; benefits to year 3
teach.caption: These four headings are confirmed by the official sample rationales and are the favourite targets of business case matching sets.

teach.h: The two approaches that sit beside the business case
teach.body: The benefits management approach defines the actions and benefits reviews that will confirm the benefits are realized, including measures, timing, responsibilities and the benefits tolerance (how far a benefit target may slip before escalation). The sustainability management approach defines the actions, reviews and controls that make sure the sustainability performance targets are met; it supports the business case and references the organization's ESG goals. Both are agreed in initiation.

teach.h: Who does what for the business case
head: Role
Area of focus (verified)
rows: Issues the mandate; identifies the executive
Secures funding; owns the business case
Specifies benefits; shows they are on track
Prepares and updates the business case
Consulted on the full business case
teach.caption: Prepare the full business case (15.4.5): executive accountable, project manager responsible, project assurance consulted, business layer not involved.
The senior user's commitment continues after closure through handover, adoption and benefits realization.

teach.text: Classic confusion: the executive is accountable for the business case, but it is the senior user who specifies the benefits and demonstrates to the business that the forecast benefits are on track, including after the project closes. A benefit forecast goes under 'expected benefits'; HOW and WHEN it will be measured goes in the benefits management approach.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Fernhollow Kitchen in initiation
teach.body: Nadia Osei, the project manager, is preparing the full business case. Flat own-label sales and falling margins go under reasons. The £6 million forecast and 28% margin go under expected benefits. Eleven months to launch, with benefits tracked to year three, go under time. The £2.3 million budget and listing fee go under costs. The agreed 10% shortfall allowed on year-three sales before escalation goes in the benefits management approach; the 1.5 kg CO2e per meal target goes in the sustainability management approach.

teach.h: Answering a business case heading item
items: Strip the fact to its job: is it a why, a gain, a period, a cost, a review plan or a green target?
A why or a link to strategy is reasons; a measurable gain against today is expected benefits.
Periods for the project and for benefits are time; build, running costs and funding are costs.
How, when and by whom benefits are proved, and benefits tolerance, go in the benefits approach.
Sustainability targets, tolerances and controls go in the sustainability approach.
Business case headings: reasons, expected benefits, time, costs (5.5).
Benefits tolerance and benefits reviews: benefits management approach (5.2.2).
Sustainability targets and controls: sustainability management approach (5.2.2).
Executive secures funding and owns the business case; senior user specifies benefits and shows they are on track.
Full business case: PM responsible, executive accountable, assurance consulted (15.4.5).

summary: You can now place scenario facts under the right business case heading or in the benefits or sustainability management approach. You can also match business case actions to the business layer, executive, senior user and project manager.

A.q: At Fernhollow Foods, project manager Nadia Osei is preparing the full business case for the Fernhollow Kitchen launch during initiation. She has this statement: 'Own-label sales have been flat for three years and margins are falling, so the company needs a brand of its own to grow.' Under which business case heading should it be recorded?
A.why: Reasons explains why the project is being undertaken and how it enables business objectives. Flat sales and falling margins are the reason for building an own brand (5.5).

whyNot.0: Expected benefits are measurable improvements against today, such as a sales target; this statement explains the need, not a gain.
whyNot.1: Costs summarize project costs, running costs and funding; no money is described here.
whyNot.3: Time covers the period of the project and of benefits realization; the statement gives no period.

A.q: Fernhollow Foods is in initiation for its Fernhollow Kitchen range. The sales and marketing team forecasts £6 million of branded sales a year by year three, against no branded sales today, with a gross margin of 28%. Where should this forecast be recorded?
A.why: Expected benefits are stated in measurable terms against the situation before the project. A sales and margin forecast against a zero baseline is exactly that (5.5).

whyNot.0: The benefits management approach sets out how and when benefits will be measured and reviewed, not the forecast itself.
whyNot.2: The project product description defines the major products, quality expectations and acceptance criteria, not financial gains.
whyNot.3: Reasons explain why the project is needed; a measurable forecast gain belongs under expected benefits.

A.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is two stages into delivery. The managing director asks who on the project board should demonstrate to the business that the forecast £6 million of branded sales is still on track to be realized. Which role should do this?
A.why: The senior user specifies the benefits and demonstrates to the business that the forecast benefits in the business case are on track to being realized (6.2.4.2).

whyNot.0: The senior supplier commits supplier resources and is accountable for the quality of supplier products, not for benefits.
whyNot.1: The project manager maintains the business case on the executive's behalf but does not answer to the business for benefits.
whyNot.2: The executive owns the business case and secures funding, but demonstrating benefit forecasts is the senior user's responsibility.

B.q: During initiation of Fernhollow Kitchen, the project board agrees that year-three branded sales may fall up to 10% short of the £6 million forecast before the shortfall must be escalated. Where should this be recorded?
options: The business case, under expected benefits
B.why: Benefits tolerance, the permissible deviation in a benefit target before escalation, is documented in the benefits management approach (5.2.2).

whyNot.0: Expected benefits hold the forecast gains themselves; the allowed shortfall before escalation is benefits tolerance.
whyNot.1: The sustainability management approach holds sustainability targets and tolerances, not sales benefits.
whyNot.3: The project plan carries plan-level tolerances such as time and cost; benefits tolerance is documented in the benefits approach.

B.q: Fernhollow's board wants a carbon label on every pack with no more than 1.5 kg CO2e per meal. Nadia Osei must record this target together with the checks and reviews that will show it is being met. Which product should hold it?
options: The business case, under expected benefits
B.why: The sustainability management approach defines the actions, reviews and controls that ensure the sustainability performance targets are achieved (5.2.2, 5.5).

whyNot.1: The benefits management approach covers benefits actions and reviews, not sustainability targets.
whyNot.2: The quality management approach covers quality techniques, standards and responsibilities, not sustainability performance targets.
whyNot.3: Expected benefits list measurable gains; sustainability targets and the controls and reviews that check them are documented in the sustainability management approach.

B.q: Fernhollow's £2.3 million budget will be funded partly from reserves and partly from a new bank facility, and the bank needs a named person on the project to commit the company to the borrowing. Which role should secure this funding?
B.why: The executive secures funding for the project and is responsible for the business case and continued business justification (6.2.4.1).

whyNot.0: The senior user specifies benefits and represents users; securing funding is the executive's area.
whyNot.2: The project manager prepares and maintains the business case but does not secure funding.
whyNot.3: The business layer issues the mandate and identifies the executive; within the project, the executive secures the funding.

C.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Nadia Osei, the project manager, updates the outline business case with the time and cost from the project plan and the aggregated risks, consults project assurance, and then asks the executive to sign it off as the full business case. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the project manager is responsible and the executive accountable for it
Yes, because the senior user is responsible for realizing the benefits after closure
No, because the executive should prepare the full business case personally
No, because the business layer is accountable for approving the full business case
C.why: In 'prepare the full business case' (15.4.5) the project manager is responsible, the executive accountable and project assurance consulted. Nadia's actions match that RACI.

whyNot.1: It is true that the senior user is responsible for the continued realization of benefits after closure, but that does not explain who prepares and signs off the full business case.
whyNot.2: The executive owns the business case, but preparing it is the project manager's responsibility on the executive's behalf.
whyNot.3: The business layer is not involved in this activity; the project board approves the business case when authorizing the project.

C.q: At Fernhollow Foods, the managing director asks Nadia Osei to write into the business case's 'expected benefits' heading the plan for measuring branded sales at 12, 24 and 36 months after launch, and who will carry out each review. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because expected benefits must be measurable against today's position
Yes, because the time heading covers the period for realizing benefits
No, because the project team should carry out the reviews before closure
No, because the benefits management approach defines the benefits reviews
C.why: How, when and by whom benefits will be measured and reviewed belongs in the benefits management approach, which defines the benefits actions and reviews (5.5).

whyNot.0: It is true that expected benefits are measurable, but the review schedule and reviewers are not benefits; they belong in the benefits management approach.
whyNot.1: It is true that the time heading covers the benefit period, but that does not make a review plan an expected benefit.
whyNot.2: Post-project benefits reviews are planned by the project but carried out by the business after closure, so this reason is wrong.

C.q: Fernhollow Kitchen has reached the end of the concept and recipe stage. The project manager asks the senior user to update the business case with actual costs to date and the latest forecasts before the board decides on the next stage. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the senior user specifies the benefits in the business case
Yes, because the senior user shows the business that benefits are on track
No, because the project manager updates the business case at each stage end
No, because the business case is updated in the closing a project process
C.why: The maintain step has the project manager update the business case at the end of each stage with progress data and the latest forecasts, ready for the board's check (5.3.1, 'update the business case' in managing a stage boundary).

whyNot.0: It is true that the senior user specifies benefits, but maintaining the whole business case at stage ends is the project manager's job.
whyNot.1: It is true that the senior user demonstrates benefit forecasts are on track, but that does not make them the person who updates the business case.
whyNot.3: The business case is updated in closing, but it is also updated at every stage boundary, so this is not the reason.

reteach.title: Four drawers, one question each
reteach.question: If you picture four labelled drawers, which question does each one answer?

blocks.h: Ask what the fact is for
blocks.body: The business case answers 'is this worth it?' through reasons, expected benefits, time and costs. The benefits management approach answers 'how will we prove the gains, and how far can they slip?'. The sustainability management approach answers 'what are our green targets and how do we control them?'. The project brief answers 'is there enough to start initiation?'.

steps.label: Senior user
steps.sub: Shows the board it is on track

blocks.text: A review plan or a tolerance is not a benefit. The forecast lives in the business case; how it is checked and how far it may slip live in the benefits management approach.

explain.body: Reasons: why the project is needed and how it serves business objectives. Expected benefits: measurable gains against the pre-project position. Time: how long the project runs and over what period benefits come. Costs: project costs, ongoing running and maintenance costs, and funding.

test.q: Fernhollow Foods' business case must show that the £2.3 million budget will come from company reserves and a bank facility, and that the new tray-sealing line will cost about £40,000 a year to maintain. Under which heading should this be recorded?
test.why: Costs summarize the project costs, the ongoing operations and maintenance costs and their funding arrangements (5.5).

whyNot.0: Time covers the project and benefit periods, not funding.
whyNot.1: Reasons explain why the project is needed.
whyNot.2: Expected benefits are measurable gains, not money spent.

explain.body: It defines the benefits management actions and benefits reviews that confirm benefits are realized, with measures, timing, responsibilities and the benefits tolerance. It is created in initiation and updated at stage boundaries and in closing, when post-project reviews are planned.

test.q: Before closing Fernhollow Kitchen, Nadia Osei must make sure that the reviews of branded sales after launch are planned, with dates and the people who will carry them out. Which product should she update?
test.why: Post-project benefits reviews are planned by updating the benefits management approach in closing (5.5, 19.2).

whyNot.1: The lessons report passes on lessons, not benefits review plans.
whyNot.2: The end project report reviews performance against the baselined PID.
whyNot.3: The sustainability approach covers sustainability targets, not sales benefits.

explain.body: It defines the actions, reviews and controls that ensure the project's sustainability performance targets are achieved, documents sustainability targets and tolerances, supports the business case and references the organization's ESG goals.

test.q: Fernhollow's board agrees that the carbon footprint may exceed 1.5 kg CO2e per meal by up to 0.1 kg before the project manager must escalate. Where should this limit be documented?
options: The business case, under expected benefits
test.why: Sustainability performance targets and tolerances are documented in the sustainability management approach (5.2.2).

whyNot.0: Benefits tolerance, not sustainability tolerance, sits in the benefits approach.
whyNot.1: The quality approach covers quality standards, techniques and responsibilities.
whyNot.3: Expected benefits hold measurable gains, not the limits on a sustainability target.

explain.body: The executive is the single point of accountability: secures funding and owns the business case and continued justification. The senior user specifies the benefits, demonstrates that forecasts are on track and keeps responsibility for realizing benefits after closure.

test.q: Fernhollow's board is choosing who should specify the benefits the new range must deliver and keep realizing them once the range passes to the normal sales team after closure. Which role is this?
test.why: The senior user specifies benefits and is responsible for benefits realization, including after closure (6.2.4.2).

whyNot.0: The executive owns the business case and funding, not benefit specification.
whyNot.1: The senior supplier represents suppliers and product quality.
whyNot.2: The project manager's role ends at closure and does not include realizing benefits.
